items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Taiwanese analyst: the Huang scandal is a detonator, the target is chip leakage
items.idea: Andrew Lu (translated by Jukan) argues Washington gets three things from the Huang scandal: Huang's anti-sanction lobbying loses legitimacy, H200 approvals for China get reversed after the NYT found 'ghost office' buyers, and Nvidia gets a congressional watchdog via the independent board probe. Closed-door hearing is Nov 18, earnings Nov 17. Innes flags it as theory not fact but says policy, not the scandal, alters cash flows.
items.angle: China revenue optionality in NVDA is the thing to haircut. The 'who benefits' framing matters more than the affair itself.
items.tweetA: The affair is the headline. The real print is whether H200 licences get pulled before Nov 17. If China is already zero in the numbers, the stock reacts to guidance on everything else. If not, it doesn't. Check the bridge.
items.tweetB: Huang spent two years as the best lobbyist against a full China chip ban. One intelligence leak later, he can't say the word 'China' in Congress. Strange way to win an export-control fight. $NVDA $AMD

items.title: 'AI is a Honeypot Story': Huang's access to Trump overlapped with the affair window
items.idea: Alice Huang (Megaspeed, Singapore) relationship ran mid-2024 to early 2026. Per Business Insider, Megaspeed's Malaysian sister bought roughly $4.8B of Nvidia hardware Jun 2024-Feb 2026. S&P futures erased about $300B implied at Sunday open. Culper Research's May 13 40-page 'The China Problem' flagged it six months ago. Three House committee chairs want a closed briefing Nov 18; Trump says 'honorable guy'.
items.angle: Short-seller flagged the risk in May. Governance premium for a key-person name. Singapore/Malaysia as the compute-laundering route is the new regulatory target.
items.tweetA: Culper published a 40-page 'NVIDIA: The China Problem' on May 13. Market ignored it for six months and punished it in six hours. Risk that is public but unpriced is still unpriced. $NVDA
items.tweetB: $4.8B of Nvidia hardware into a Malaysian affiliate of one Singapore firm. Now ask how many other Megaspeeds exist before Commerce does. The next export rule is about data center ownership, not chips. $SMCI $DELL

items.source: David Rosenberg / Early Morning with Dave
items.title: 'The AI Boom Has Peaked': Huang espionage story lands on an already stressed AI trade
items.idea: Rosenberg's key takeaway: Huang acknowledged being the target of a foreign espionage effort via a relationship with an executive suspected of working for Chinese intelligence; board probe launched, NVDA -5% overnight on top of 'severe pressure' from doubts about AI boom sustainability. Headline calls the boom over; midterms framed as a referendum on data construction (data centers). Only the intro was in the email body.
items.angle: Rosenberg is the loudest top-call voice in the inbox today. Compare with Dauber's 60/40 for mechanical liquidation.
items.tweetA: Rosenberg says the AI boom has peaked. Dauber puts it 60/40 it was only a mechanical liquidation. Both read the same tape. The tell is HY spread and CoreWeave CDS, not NVDA. $HYG $CRWV
items.tweetB: Midterms as a referendum on data centers, plus a CEO scandal, plus a -5% gap. When three unrelated shocks hit one trade the same week, it stops being idiosyncratic. It's positioning. Who is still long and unhedged?

items.title: Vol-control funds sold $101B of S&P on Nov 5, the biggest day since at least 2015
items.idea: Vol-targeting books went from $286B to $157B in three sessions. Another 4% down day forces only about $27B more. Equal weight beat cap-weight by 147bp on Thursday's 4.36% fall, the largest relative gain on a 3%+ decline since 1990 (Citadel Securities). Trend followers are -1.40% of risk in Nasdaq futures vs +0.81% a month ago, as short as the April 2025 and April 2026 lows. Retail sold $1.9B in the first half hour then bought every half hour into the close.
items.angle: Mechanical sellers are exhausted: that is the bull argument in one paragraph. Gives a quantified floor on forced supply.
items.tweetA: Vol-control funds already dumped $101B and have $27B left to sell on another 4% drop. The forced seller is mostly done. The question is who is the discretionary seller. $SPY $QQQ
items.tweetB: Equal weight beat the index by 147bp on a 4.4% down day. Biggest ever since 1990. That's not a panic signature. That's a de-gross. Different trade, different recovery.

items.title: Credit is the tile that hasn't stood back up: HY 348bp, tech CDS ~650bp
items.idea: HY printed 348bp for Nov 5, +16bp, the sixth print over 325bp. Tech-sector 5-year protection jumped to about 650bp, highest since 2009 (peak near 900bp). CoreWeave 5y CDS trades over 1,000bp. Equities fell first and spreads followed one session later. Dauber stays short lenders and the HY fund; wrong if next print is back inside 325bp; the 355bp line and CoreWeave widening decide whether 'the bounce is a loan'.
items.angle: Cleanest cross-asset tell for the AI buildout financing question. CRWV CDS above 1,000bp is a funding-cost signal.
items.tweetA: Tech sector CDS at 650bp is the highest since 2009. Equity bounced Friday. Spreads usually follow with a one-session lag. If HY prints over 355bp Monday the bounce was a loan. $HYG $JNK $CRWV
items.tweetB: CoreWeave five-year protection over 1,000bp, in a week CoreWeave reports. Nvidia sells GPUs to CoreWeave, CoreWeave borrows against those GPUs. Where does the circle break first?

items.title: Payrolls +165k vs 59k expected: December hike 77% priced, CPI Tuesday decides
items.idea: Oct payrolls beat by over 100k; 2y +5bp to 4.51%, 10y only +2bp (flattening). Dauber likes JPM over BAC, wrong if core CPI prints 0.2% or less and the 2y approaches 4.40%. Compare Innes, who quotes payrolls at 159k with 84k of upward revisions and expects 0.2% core. 2018 analog: S&P fell 19% Sep peak to Dec 24, with a hike Dec 19 then shutdown three days later; this year hike decision Dec 9, funding deadline Dec 11.
items.angle: Two newsletters quote different payroll numbers (165k vs 159k). Note the discrepancy. The 2018 calendar overlay is the tweetable bit.
items.tweetA: 2018: hike Dec 19, shutdown Dec 22, S&P -19% peak to trough. 2026: hike decision Dec 9, funding deadline Dec 11. Same calendar rhymes, but this time the AI complex is already down. $SPY $TLT
items.tweetB: Hike 77% priced, 2y at 4.51%, curve flattening on a strong print. The bond market is saying hike now, growth later. That's the opposite of what equity bulls need ahead of CPI.

items.title: Hormuz transits at ~1% of normal on day 253; noon Trump-Qatar meeting is the oil swing
items.idea: Brent near $94.75. Cabinet split three ways: Vance wants war ended, CENTCOM (Cooper) and Hegseth want major combat back, Rubio and Bessent want the blockade held. Tehran's 'two-day proposal': strait reopens if the US ends the blockade, lifts sanctions, cuts forces and unfreezes assets. Israel Hayom: about $8B of frozen funds offered for the strait, nuclear program left out. Dauber owns no oil; wrong if meeting yields a dated transit accord. CENTCOM also stood up an Iran land/Caspian routes task force.
items.angle: Brent was -16% last week per Innes on settlement hopes, with transit still 1% of normal. That gap is the trade.
items.tweetA: Hormuz at 1% of normal for 253 days and Brent is $95, down 16% last week on hope. Either the strait reopens soon, or the market is pricing the wrong tail. $XLE $OXY
items.tweetB: Three factions in the cabinet, three different oil outcomes: end the war, resume combat, hold the blockade. Whoever walks out of the Qatar meeting with Trump sets crude for the week. I'd rather be long optionality than a view.

items.title: Rest of the tape: Kirishi refinery on fire, Khor Mor shut, Russian military dead near 400k
items.idea: Ukrainian drones set Russia's second-largest refinery (Kirishi) on fire; a drone attack shut Iraq's Khor Mor gas field. Hacked Rosstat data put Russian military deaths in Ukraine near 400,000 (Bloomberg). China extended the tariff pause on US goods by two months to Jan 10. Herzog gave Eisenkot the mandate to form an Israeli government (67 recommendations vs Netanyahu's 46) with 28 days plus 14.
items.angle: Refinery and gas outages stack on top of Hormuz. Israel coalition math is the next oil tile per Dauber.
items.tweetA: Russia's #2 refinery on fire, Iraq's Khor Mor gas field shut, Hormuz at 1% transit. Product cracks have three separate supply shocks and the equity market is debating Nvidia's CEO. $VLO $MPC
items.tweetB: 400,000 Russian military dead, per hacked Rosstat data. The Kremlin spent years hiding that number. It is the demographic story of the decade for a country already shrinking.

items.title: Fed seat politics: a Democratic Senate can leave Cook's seat empty, stalling Bowman's bank-capital easing
items.idea: WSJ via Dauber: if Trump fires Lisa Cook, a Democratic Senate could leave the seat unfilled, which means Michelle Bowman's push to ease big-bank capital would need Democratic votes. Also: boardrooms running a 'now or never' push on large mergers before January, with SpaceX and Tesla as the test case (Bloomberg). Stephen Miller starts as chief of staff today; Massie can force a House vote on impeaching Hegseth within two legislative days.
items.angle: Bank deregulation tail risk reprices from Jan 3 when Democrats take both chambers. Merger rush is a time-boxed catalyst.
items.tweetA: Blue Congress starts Jan 3. Bank capital easing now needs Democratic votes if Cook's seat stays empty. Banks pricing deregulation as a done deal should check the calendar. $JPM $BAC $GS
items.tweetB: Boards are rushing large mergers before January. Antitrust leverage flips on Jan 3. The 'now or never' M&A window is a clock, not a boom.

items.title: Nvidia took 157 index points, 35% of the S&P move from Oct 7 to Nov 5; chips -14.4%, software -10.8% on Thursday
items.idea: Nvidia alone took 157 points off the S&P between Oct 7 and Nov 5, 35% of the move. Market factor moved 5.5 sigma, value rose 3.4 sigma. TSMC +6.5%, SK Hynix +4.7%, Samsung +2.9% overnight after SOX +4.21% Friday; memory basket still -51% from June after 136 days, vs a 44% drawdown in 2025 that took 14 months to recover. IonQ, Oklo, IREN each +20% pre-market, Karman +42%.
items.angle: Single-stock index contribution is the concentration story in one number. Squeeze in money-losing small caps is crowding evidence (Apollo chart: unprofitable small caps +85% since Apr 2025 vs +35%).
items.tweetA: One stock explained 35% of the S&P drawdown. Eight percent index weight, a third of the move. 'Diversified' equity exposure is a call on one CEO and one earnings date, Nov 17. $NVDA $SPY
items.tweetB: Memory basket is down 51% in 136 days. The 2025 drawdown of 44% took 14 months to recover. Which clock are we on? Nobody in the thread asks what changed in unit demand.

items.title: Hyperscaler free cash flow turned: $14B burn over nine months vs $143.5B FCF a year earlier
items.idea: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle spent $14B more than they generated in operating cash over nine months, against $143.5B of free cash flow a year earlier (Reuters). This is Dauber's 'case against' the pure liquidation reading: the reset and the liquidation are one event at two speeds. Earnings this week: CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cisco as the funding test.
items.angle: Swing of roughly $157B in free cash. This is the capex-eats-FCF number behind the credit widening.
items.tweetA: $143.5B of free cash flow a year ago, minus $14B now, for the five biggest AI spenders. That's a $157B swing in twelve months. The buyback bid that held the index up is funding capex instead. $MSFT $GOOGL $AMZN $META $ORCL
items.tweetB: When the five hyperscalers burn cash, the marginal buyer of their stock changes, and the marginal issuer of debt changes too. Watch IG tech issuance, not NVDA.

items.title: Power names report first read since 46 of 47 data center measures restricted buildouts
items.idea: Voters restricted data center permits in 46 of 47 decided measures (Dauber elsewhere says 'all but one passed'). Constellation Energy and NRG report before the open as the first power read since the referenda. Occidental and Take-Two after the close. Also: average US stock fund lost 1.3% in October while IG bond funds made 2.3% (WSJ).
items.angle: Test case for whether the nuclear/IPP premium depends on data center demand growth.
items.tweetA: 46 of 47 ballot measures against data centers. Constellation and NRG report this morning and sell power to the exact customers voters just blocked. Guidance language is the whole trade. $CEG $NRG $VST
items.tweetB: Equity funds lost 1.3% in October, IG bond funds made 2.3%. The 60/40 hedge worked for one month. Pay attention to how many portfolios were not positioned for that.

items.title: Nvidia sits in ~900-1,000 ETFs at ~8% of the S&P; Huang story is an ETF plumbing story
items.idea: Boockvar: Nvidia market cap is about 8% of the S&P 500, and per Gemini/Grok it is held in nearly 900 to 1,000 major US and core ETFs. The direction of the stock matters for the index and thousands of other funds. Contrast Dauber's 35% of drawdown attribution and AI Supremacy's top-10 weight of 37-40%.
items.angle: Passive ownership translates a single-name governance shock into forced beta everywhere.
items.tweetA: Nvidia is in roughly 900-1,000 ETFs. A board probe into one CEO now touches every target-date fund and every 'diversified' index. That's not idiosyncratic risk anymore, it's plumbing. $NVDA $SPY $VOO
items.tweetB: Top 10 stocks are ~37-40% of the S&P. One of them is under a board investigation. The other nine are the AI capex complex. Diversification across that basket is mostly a naming convention.

items.title: Anthropic S-1: $895.4B committed spend vs $35.3B trailing revenue (25x)
items.idea: Per S-1 quoted via Michael Burry: aggregate committed spend about $895.4B, 25x TTM revenue of $35.3B, 13x Q3 annualized revenue, 12-13x the $69-74B end-September run-rate. $447.5B is expected before Dec 31, 2030 (about 13x sales inside 17 quarters). $69.8B due in the 12 months to Sep 30, 2027 vs Q3 annualized revenue of $67.8B. October run-rate left blank in the updated S-1. Boockvar: Anthropic must raise this money, IPO or private.
items.angle: Commitments due in year one roughly equal annualized revenue. The cash call is the IPO rationale.
items.tweetA: Anthropic discloses $69.8B of compute commitments due inside twelve months. Annualized revenue: $67.8B. Every dollar of growth is already spoken for before it's earned. The IPO isn't optional. $NVDA $AMZN $GOOGL $ORCL
items.tweetB: $895B of commitments is 25x trailing revenue. In S-1 terms that's a take-or-pay book behind a business doing $67.8B annualized. Who is on the other side of those contracts? The same names whose free cash flow just went negative. $MSFT $ORCL

items.title: Anthropic IPO bull case: every company becomes a subsidiary of a frontier AI lab
items.idea: Noah's thesis: success in any industry will require tying your capital structure to a frontier AI company with an internal proprietary model months ahead of distilled versions, making firms de facto subsidiaries of Anthropic, OpenAI or Google. Cites Imas, Koh and Legg (2026, Google DeepMind): when AI coordination improves it can 'break the Coasean ceiling' on firm size, leading to a phase transition toward large concentrated AI-heavy firms. Brad DeLong and Dan Wang are more skeptical on the 67-minute video. Noah will probably buy at IPO.
items.angle: A conglomerate-structure thesis rather than a displacement thesis. Frames the $895B commitments as vertical integration capex.
items.tweetA: Noah's Anthropic bull case isn't 'AI replaces workers.' It's that every firm becomes a subsidiary of one of three labs. If true, the commitments in the S-1 buy a keiretsu, not a SaaS product. Value it like Mitsubishi, not like Salesforce. $GOOGL $MSFT
items.tweetB: DeepMind economists just published a model where better AI coordination breaks the Coasean ceiling on firm size. A lab publishing the theory for its own conglomerate future is either research or a business plan.

items.title: Hexapodia returns as Substack Live: DeLong and Dan Wang skeptical on Anthropic
items.idea: The Hexapodia podcast relaunches as Substack Live recordings. Anthropic IPO debate: Noah bullish, Dan Wang (China tech/industrial policy) and Brad DeLong more skeptical. Noah also discloses he owns stock in TypeSafe, an Anthropic competitor. Disclosure style is a signal of how personal-finance writing around an IPO is changing.
items.angle: Media format shift: newsletter-to-live-to-podcast loop as an IPO narrative engine.
items.tweetA: The Anthropic IPO narrative is being priced on Substack Live before the roadshow. Retail has the S-1 on day one and three economists debating it for an hour. That's a different book-building process. $PRIVATE
items.tweetB: Noah will 'probably buy at IPO.' Dan Wang and Brad DeLong are skeptical. When the pundit class splits publicly before the pricing, the allocation fight is partly a narrative fight.

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: FX Daily: DXY back above 102, Innes short AUD/JPY ahead of CPI
items.idea: DXY reclaimed post-election losses, 101.10 on Nov 4 to above 102. October payrolls +159k with +84k revisions; 3-month average 137k vs 28k the prior quarter; 2026 average 86k vs 10k in 2025. Wages ~3.1% y/y, unemployment a little above 4%. 70k professional and business services jobs undercut the 'AI is hollowing out white collar' story. About 20bp of December tightening priced. EUR/USD 2.1-2.3% below rate-differential fair value; move above 1.120 plausible.
items.angle: Payroll strength with soft wages is a stagflation-lite print. The euro-gap number is a mean-reversion setup.
items.tweetA: Payrolls averaged 86k a month this year vs 10k in 2025. Professional services added 70k. If AI were eating white-collar jobs, that is the last line item you'd see rising. $UUP $EURUSD
items.tweetB: Euro is 2.1-2.3% below where rate differentials say it should be, and French risk can't explain all of it. Dollar bulls need a CPI surprise to extend. Core 0.2% and the whole post-election dollar leg unwinds. $FXE

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Brent -16% last week: oil as a quiet disinflation lever for the Fed
items.idea: Innes: Brent's roughly 16% decline last week on Washington-Tehran settlement hopes could do some of the Fed's work if it lasts. But the benefit would not be US-only; other central banks could reassess, so FX response depends on relative rate expectations. He also notes gold's positive correlation with equities: another AI liquidation could pull bullion lower as investors raise cash. 'The margin clerk rarely cares whether the asset being sold is supposed to be a safe haven.'
items.angle: Contrast with Dauber: Brent still near $95 with Hormuz at 1% transit. Gold-as-liquidity-source is a trade risk for the gold book.
items.tweetA: Brent -16% in a week with Hormuz at 1% of normal. Either physical flows resume or the paper market is front-running a deal that hasn't been signed. The Fed will not wait to find out. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: If tech liquidates again, gold sells too. Correlation to equities is the thing nobody models when they call it the safe haven. Margin clerks don't read fundamentals. $GLD $GC

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: SpaceX lock-up clock: Goldman's Snider sees an $11B passive bid from a December index rebalance
items.idea: Largest US IPO in history is approaching a supply/demand test. Goldman's Ben Snider identifies a December index rebalance that could bring about $11B of mechanical demand into SpaceX as lock-ups expire. The unknown is how much stock newly unlocked insiders will sell into that bid. A much larger index opportunity sits further out and needs different conditions. Only the intro was in the email body.
items.angle: Passive bid vs insider supply is a defined-date flow trade. Dauber flags SpaceX/Tesla as the merger test case.
items.tweetA: $11B of passive demand arriving in December, against a growing pile of unlocked insider shares. The index rebalance is a date. The selling is a choice. I'd want to know the lock-up schedule before I know the bid. $TSLA
items.tweetB: SpaceX is going to be a benchmark weight before most people have valued it. When passive buys a name at any price, price discovery moves to the sellers. Who is selling and why?

items.title: Final 401(k) alternatives rule reaches the White House, a path for crypto in retirement plans
items.idea: DOL sent the final 401(k) alternatives rule to OIRA on Nov 5, flagged economically significant. March 31 proposal: fiduciaries weighing six factors including fees, liquidity and valuation get a judgment 'presumed reasonable and entitled to significant deference'. Warren, Sanders and Rep. Scott urged rescission on June 1. Reached White House review 157 days after comments closed. Final text not public.
items.angle: Retirement-plan access is the largest structural crypto flow story. The Democratic Congress arrives Jan 3, so timing matters.
items.tweetA: The 401(k) rule is at OIRA. Democrats take both chambers Jan 3. That gives the White House about eight weeks to finalize a rule that Warren wanted rescinded. Watch the Federal Register, not the CT timeline. $BTC $COIN $IBIT
items.tweetB: The proposal doesn't mention crypto by name. It just says fiduciaries get a presumption of reasonableness on alternatives. That is how you open a retirement-plan door without a single political fight on the word 'Bitcoin'.

items.title: FinCEN and Fed withdraw the 2020 Travel Rule proposal ($3,000 to $250), crypto language gone
items.idea: FinCEN and the Fed withdrew the 2020 proposal that would have cut the Travel Rule threshold for international transfers from $3,000 to $250 and defined 'money' to cover convertible virtual currency. Announced Nov 6, published in the Federal Register Monday. Drew nearly 3,000 comments, mostly opposed. Agencies cited market maturation and the GENIUS Act, and promised no final rule without further comment.
items.angle: Biggest regulatory overhang on self-custody and cross-border stablecoin flows removed. Pair with Nigeria's central bank licensing move below.
items.tweetA: FinCEN killed the $250 Travel Rule threshold after six years. The reason it gave is the GENIUS Act. Stablecoin law replaced the surveillance proposal. That's the regime change nobody tweeted about. $USDC $CRCL
items.tweetB: 3,000 comments, six years, one withdrawal. The agency's own language: 'no final rule without an additional opportunity for public comment.' That reads like a promise to the next Congress, not just to industry.

items.title: Binance CFO Kaiser Ng quits nine days after a ~$6.3B hot-wallet drain; EU accounts closing
items.idea: Ng leaves to found a real-world-asset tokenization startup (sports, GPUs, gold); CZ says YZi Labs is 'always keen to back' former colleagues. Justin Yek from Airwallex takes over as CFO. This follows attackers draining about $6.3B from Binance's hot wallets nine days ago. Separately: Binance is closing accounts in France, Spain, Italy and Poland on Dec 31 with a fee of the greater of 0.025% or 10 USDC from Nov 29, and Binance-controlled Korean exchange GOPAX halted trading Nov 6 and requires emails to withdraw (Binance holds 67.45% of operator Streami).
items.angle: A $6.3B hot-wallet loss, a CFO exit, EU offboarding and a Korean affiliate freeze in nine days. Counterparty risk is the trade.
items.tweetA: $6.3B drained from Binance hot wallets. CFO out nine days later. EU users offboarded by Dec 31. A Korean affiliate in withdrawal-by-email mode. The 'transition plan' language is doing a lot of work. Where is your exchange balance? $BNB $BTC
items.tweetB: Chainalysis, Web3Auth/Keplr, Gnosis Pay, Binance: four security incidents in one newsletter. The common thread isn't crypto, it's the compliance and key-management stack. The picks-and-shovels of custody are the story. $COIN

items.title: Treasury cuts MEXC off from US finance: $16B in alleged sanctions evasion, $1.5B Russia and $1B Iran
items.idea: FinCEN order targets MEXC for alleged ties to at least $16B in sanctions evasion and illicit activity 2021-2026, including about $1.5B Russia-linked and about $1B Iran-linked transactions. Same newsletter notes Nigeria's central bank now requires offshore stablecoin issuers to incorporate, license and hold 10B naira minimum capital (existing operators have until May 4, 2027). Both are chokepoint moves on exchange and issuer layers.
items.angle: Enforcement is moving from exchanges to stablecoin issuers globally. Iran-linked flows during an active US-Iran standoff.
items.tweetA: $1B of Iran-linked transactions through one exchange while the US negotiates over Hormuz. Treasury picking this week to name MEXC is not accidental. Crypto rails are now a sanctions-enforcement front. $USDT
items.tweetB: Nigeria wants offshore stablecoin issuers to incorporate locally, 10B naira capital. The US wants them onshore under GENIUS. The emerging market rule is the same as the US one: license or leave. Tether has a decision to make. $USDT $CRCL

items.title: Strive posts $509M Q3 net income on a $533.7M BTC gain; holds 43,124 BTC
items.idea: Strive reported $509M net income for Q3, driven by a $533.7M unrealized gain on bitcoin. It held 43,124 BTC as of Oct 30 after buying 15,124 BTC in October alone. WLFI announced a buyback to 'consolidate voting power' with no size or date. Vitalik says ETH should focus on store of value rather than maximizing fee burn. Bitwise CIO Hougan says 'no sellers left' after a 3.7% inflation print, the Binance hack and a Democratic sweep all failed to break the market.
items.angle: A treasury company bought 35% of its holdings in a single month. Hougan's 'no sellers left' is a positioning claim worth testing.
items.tweetA: Strive bought 15,124 BTC in October, a third of its stack in one month, in a month BTC held up through a hack, 3.7% inflation and a blue sweep. If that isn't an absorption signal, what is? $BTC $ASST
items.tweetB: Vitalik: don't maximize ETH fee burn, it would cost decentralization. ETH as store of value, not as a yield instrument. The treasury-company bid and the base-layer philosophy are pulling in different directions. $ETH

items.title: Texas data-center pause vs bitcoin miners; ex-FBI agent stole $2.47M in crypto from 35 cases
items.idea: Recommended reads: David Okoya on which bitcoin miners are already past the Texas data-center freeze (the vote intersects with the AI-hosting pivot of miners); Alex Thorn on how a Democratic victory alters crypto and AI policy. Ex-FBI agent Patrick Yaroch pleaded guilty to stealing about $2.47M in crypto from wallets tied to 35 FBI cases, over twice what he told the FBI in July. Aave Labs acquired the Avon team for fixed-rate lending.
items.angle: Miner-to-AI-hosting pivot now carries political risk in Texas. Aave fixed-rate lending is a DeFi product-cycle datapoint.
items.tweetA: Miners pivoted to AI hosting for the premium. Texas voted to pause new data centers. Which miners are grandfathered is now the whole valuation question. $IREN $CORZ $RIOT
items.tweetB: Aave buying a team to build fixed-rate lending is the DeFi equivalent of the yield curve arriving. Rates infrastructure follows leverage demand. Watch the onchain order book piece. $AAVE

items.title: RDVT: $165.7M cash, zero debt, but $46.1M of unrecorded exec SBC tied to 2030 targets
items.idea: Red Violet Q3 revenue +20% to $27.75M, over $100M LTM for the first time. After an Aug raise of ~1.92M shares at $60 ($108.7M net) it holds $165.66M cash with zero debt. Execs got 832,690 RSUs (~$43.9M fair value) tied to revenue and adj. EBITDA margin through March 2030, none expensed as 'not probable' under ASC 718; total unrecorded SBC $46.14M, a potential ~6% dilution charge. Capitalized software is ~15% of revenue vs the 5% norm; fair value $55 per Hermit's DCF.
items.angle: Hidden SBC reading is a template for small-cap data names. A 20% grower with a 15% capitalized-software ratio is a quality-of-earnings flag.
items.tweetA: Red Violet capitalizes software at roughly 15% of revenue. Software norm is closer to 5%. GAAP margin looks better; cash tells a different story. And $46M of exec SBC hasn't touched the P&L yet. $RDVT
items.tweetB: Zero expense recognized on $46M of performance RSUs because they are 'not probable'. The day they become probable, opex absorbs a ~6% dilution charge in one quarter. That's a quiet earnings cliff. $RDVT

items.title: RDVT: data broker in the ~150-defendant Daniel's Law suit; home healthcare is the FOREWARN playbook
items.idea: Red Violet is one of ~150 data brokers sued in New Jersey state court (Atlas Data Privacy Corp) under Daniel's Law for allegedly failing to suppress covered officials' addresses within 10 days; its liability insurance is covering defense. Growth: FOREWARN has over 50% of US Realtor Associations (>665) with 100% renewal; the plan is to replicate it in home healthcare (~4M home health aides, >12k Medicare-certified agencies), and to displace LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters CLEAR in municipal law enforcement. Management hints at M&A with a 30,000-RSU acquisition grant.
items.angle: A privacy-law class action against an entire data-broker category. Public sector displacing LexisNexis is the moat evidence.
items.tweetA: ~150 data brokers sued under one New Jersey privacy law. If statutory damages stack per record, the category has a liability nobody is modeling. Red Violet's insurer is paying for now. $RDVT
items.tweetB: A 100% renewal rate across 665 realtor associations. Now apply the same playbook to 4 million home health aides. Safety verification for in-home work is a better niche than most AI wrappers. $RDVT

items.source: Danielle DiMartino Booth / The Daily Feather
items.title: McKinsey turns 100: consultants as cost cutters and CYA, framed through Office Space's 'the Bobs'
items.idea: McKinsey & Co. turned 100 this year. DiMartino Booth frames consultants as brought in to 1) cut costs (jobs) or 2) provide cover for management ('who could blame you if McKinsey's recommendation backfires?'). Uses Office Space (shot in Dallas, 1999) 'the Bobs' as the analogy. Only the intro came through in the email body.
items.angle: Cultural frame for AI-driven headcount cuts in white-collar firms. Consultants as the human middle layer under AI pressure.
items.tweetA: McKinsey is 100 years old. The business model was: rent a credible reason to cut jobs. AI is a cheaper, faster credible reason. Which side of that trade is the consulting P&L on?
items.tweetB: Office Space's Bobs asked 'what would you say you do here?' to decide who to cut. Companies now ask an AI that same question. The radical honesty that got Peter promoted may not be an option for the model.

items.title: BUSHY portfolio -135bp last week on energy and CTA; hedges came off Thursday, 'Decision Time' on re-hedging
items.idea: The beta portfolio pulled back 135bp last week, with the energy book and the CTA allocation responsible for most of the damage. Hedges came off on Thursday and the note asks when to put them back on. Benchmarked to Vanguard's 2035 Target Date Fund. The flagship weekend note covered Chinese stocks. Most content is paywalled.
items.angle: Energy and CTA both hurt in the same week: a correlation breakdown inside a diversified book. Compare Dauber on trend followers short Nasdaq.
items.tweetA: Energy book and CTA sleeve both lost money in one week for a target-date-benchmarked portfolio. When diversifiers fail together the problem isn't the hedge. It's that the risk was never independent.
items.tweetB: Hedges came off Thursday, the day of the 4.36% drop. The cost of unhedging at the low is the hardest P&L to explain to clients. Re-hedging into a bounce is the harder discipline.

items.title: Asset allocation model avoided equities since summer, turned bullish bonds; bearish on risk for the year but another high possible
items.idea: Author is bearish on risk over the coming year but would not exclude another equity high in between: 'a true bear market will shake out both bulls and bears in the first episodes.' Asset allocation model has been out of equities since summer and turned bullish on bonds at the right time. Planning scenario work around AI cycle and monetary reaction functions. Weekly items (FX PnL sheet, calendar, dashboard, model) are behind the site.
items.angle: Systematic model ahead of the discretionary crowd on both equities and bonds. Tweetable as 'bear markets start with bull rallies'.
items.tweetA: A true bear market shakes out the bulls first and the bears second. The ones calling the top in October and covering in November are the same people who'll be short again at the lows. Positioning, not direction, is the tell.
items.tweetB: Out of equities since the summer, long bonds into the drop. A rules-based model that did the thing most discretionary desks wouldn't. The 2y at 4.51% with a hike priced is the interesting test of that bond call. $TLT $IEF

items.title: 'Default alive' test: two $15k/month hires flip a seed company from alive to dead
items.idea: Paul Graham's test applied to $2M cash, $170k/month expenses, $40k/month revenue growing 7% monthly: breakeven month 22, cash bottoms at $350k, default alive. Add two $15k hires and cash runs out in month 16; to stay alive growth must jump from 7% to 8.1%. Plan B must be dated: removing hires after 5 months bottoms at $200k, after 11 months $20k, after 12 months dead in month 20. Carta: median seed-to-A gap 1.9 years in Q4 2025; 39% took over three years in Q3 2025 vs 19% in 2019; 966 US startups shut down in 2024 vs 769 in 2023.
items.angle: Venture funding stress datapoints: seed-to-A time nearly doubled and shutdowns up 26%.
items.tweetA: Seed to Series A now takes a median of 1.9 years and 39% of companies took over three years, vs 19% in 2019. Startup shutdowns on Carta: 966 in 2024 vs 769 in 2023. The AI mega-round headlines are not the median company.
items.tweetB: Fifteen months of runway, twenty-three months to the next round. That arithmetic kills more startups than competition does. Growth math beats runway math: a $30k/month hire needs +1.1 points of monthly growth to be survivable.

items.title: 74% of SimpleClosure wind-downs since 2023 were pre-seed or seed; Carta SaaS Series A team size down to 15.9 from 19.4
items.idea: SimpleClosure found 74% of shutdowns it has handled since 2023 were pre-seed or seed companies. Carta data: SaaS companies raising a Series A in 2024 averaged 15.9 people, down from 19.4 in 2022. Only 15% get from seed to Series A within 12 months. David Sacks's counter: ask whether you are 'default investable'; Graham: if revenue grows more than ~5x a year (14.4% a month) investors stay interested.
items.angle: Smaller teams at Series A is a quiet productivity signal from AI tools. Early-stage attrition concentrated in seed.
items.tweetA: Series A SaaS teams are down to 15.9 people from 19.4 in two years. Either AI tooling is real or capital is rationing headcount. Both look identical in the data and both are bearish for white-collar hiring. $CRM
items.tweetB: 5x a year (14.4% monthly) is where investors stop caring about profitability. Our example grows 7% a month. Most seed companies are in the zone between default alive and default investable, and that zone is empty.
